research_rationale: Executive Order 8341 of February 8, 1940 (5 FR 643, Federal Register issue of Saturday, February 10, 1940; FR Doc. 40-606, filed February 9, 1940) is a single paragraph. Its only operative act is to revoke Executive Order No. 8323 of January 22, 1940, which had abolished Customs Collection District No. 43 (Tennessee), revoked the designations of Memphis, Chattanooga and Nashville as customs ports of entry, and extended the limits of Customs Collection District No. 42 (Kentucky) and Customs Collection District No. 45 (St. Louis). The held text says the earlier order "is hereby revoked." The paragraph states no later effective date, condition, report or continuing duty, so by its own terms the act was performed, and the command exhausted, when the order was signed on February 8, 1940. Identity rests on the heading, the signing date, the Federal Register document line and the page; the machine-extracted text prints the closing order-number line with a stray character and omits the number from the heading, which the packet records as a segmentation lead. The working text is the official Federal Register page text extracted from the PDF by OCR, not an authenticated transcription; page images were not inspected.
savings_reason: The revocation of Executive Order No. 8323 was carried out when Executive Order 8341 was signed on February 8, 1940. That result is a surviving effect of a completed act and is not a command that Executive Order 8341 continues to impose. The held text has no savings clause, exception or pending proceeding, and no held source shows any right or duty left outstanding by it.
earlier_end_check: No earlier end exists, because the order is itself the revocation and states no later effective date, so nothing can precede the signing date of February 8, 1940, which the held text prints as the date line. The filing date (February 9, 1940) and the issue date (February 10, 1940) are alternative readings of when the revocation became effective; each falls within the same first days of February 1940 and none changes the finding that the act was complete in February 1940. The packet's later-event chain is empty. The three machine searches (U.S. Code release point 119-121, eCFR as of 2026-10-14, and the Office of the Federal Register disposition-note catalogue) report zero hits for this order, and the bounded search of the held texts found no other held text citing it by number, so no earlier revocation, amendment or extension is shown.

research_rationale: Executive Order 8613 of December 16, 1940 (5 FR 5143, Federal Register issue of Wednesday, December 18, 1940; FR Doc. 40-5680, filed December 17, 1940) closes the executive departments and other agencies in the District of Columbia, and excuses Federal employees from duty, for the single day Tuesday, December 24, 1940, with exceptions for employees excluded by agency heads for special public reasons or whose absence would be inconsistent with existing law (paragraph 1), and directs that the order be published in the Federal Register (paragraph 2). Both paragraphs were spent by their own terms. Paragraph 2 was performed when the order appeared in the issue dated December 18, 1940; the filing line gives the earlier date December 17, 1940, which is an alternative reading. Paragraph 1 applied to one calendar day and had no subject afterwards. Following the owner ruling of 2026-10-21 on stated dates, the end of paragraph 1 is recorded as December 24, 1940, inclusive (the order runs through that day); the exclusive reading, under which it ends when December 24 begins, is the alternative. The working text is the official Federal Register page text extracted from the PDF by OCR, not an authenticated transcription; page images were not inspected.
savings_reason: The closure and the excusal from duty on December 24, 1940 took effect on that day and accrued to the employees concerned. That result is a past consequence of the executed order, not a command that Executive Order 8613 continues to impose. The held text has no savings clause, and no held source shows any right or duty extending beyond that day.
earlier_end_check: Paragraph 1 has no earlier end: no held instrument revokes, extends or amends the order (the packet's later-event chain is empty; the U.S. Code, eCFR and Office of the Federal Register disposition-note searches report zero hits; the bounded search of held texts found no other held text citing it by number). The day named in the paragraph is its own period, not a report deadline. Paragraph 2 ended earlier, by performance: the held Federal Register page for 5 FR 5143 carries the masthead of the issue dated Wednesday, December 18, 1940 and prints the order, which shows the direction to publish was carried out by that issue. The whole order therefore ended with the later of the two dates, December 24, 1940.

The inventory is complete and matches the two numbered paragraphs.
independent_command_check: No independent command exists. The exceptions in paragraph 1 qualify the closure and excusal for December 24, 1940 only and confer no standing power. Paragraph 2 is a one-time publication direction performed on publication.
savings_check: The order has no savings clause. The excused absence on December 24, 1940 is an accrued past consequence of the executed order, not a continuing command.

research_rationale: Executive Order 8639 of January 14, 1941 (6 FR 455, Federal Register issue of Friday, January 17, 1941; FR Doc. 41-383, filed January 15, 1941) revokes the designation of Unalaska, Alaska, as a customs port of entry in Customs Collection District No. 31 (Alaska), under section 1 of the Act of August 1, 1914 (38 Stat. 609, 623; 19 U.S.C. 2), and provides that the order "shall become effective at the close of business January 15, 1941." The revocation is a one-time act with a stated effective moment, so it was performed and the command exhausted at the close of business on January 15, 1941. Identity rests on the heading, the signing date of January 14, 1941, the Federal Register document line and the page; the machine-extracted text prints the closing order-number line with a stray character, which the packet records as a segmentation lead. The loss of port-of-entry status is a surviving effect of that executed act. The working text is the official Federal Register page text extracted from the PDF by OCR, not an authenticated transcription; page images were not inspected.
savings_reason: The designation of Unalaska as a customs port of entry was revoked effective at the close of business on January 15, 1941. The resulting absence of port-of-entry status is a surviving effect of the executed revocation, not a command that Executive Order 8639 continues to impose. The held text has no savings clause and no held source shows a pending right or duty under it.
earlier_end_check: No earlier end exists, because the order is itself the revocation and fixes its own effective moment, the close of business on January 15, 1941, so nothing in the order can precede that moment. The packet's later-event chain is empty. The three machine searches (U.S. Code, eCFR as of 2026-10-14, and the Office of the Federal Register disposition-note catalogue) report zero hits for this order, and the bounded search of the held texts found no other held text citing it by number. A later restoration of the designation would be a separate act and would not revive this order; none is shown in the held record. The effective-date sentence is read as ending the order's operative force at the close of that day, so the end is recorded as January 15, 1941.
scope_check: The packet inventory has one clause, the operative paragraph together with the effective-date sentence (characters 2351 to 2733 of the registered text). I compared it with the whole held order: heading, the single operative sentence, the effective-date sentence, the signature, the date line and the filing line. The effective-date sentence belongs to the same clause and fixes its end. No other clause exists.
independent_command_check: There is no independent command, delegation or continuing instruction. The only operative content is the revocation of the designation of Unalaska, and the order's own effective-date sentence fixes when that revocation takes effect.
savings_check: The order has no savings clause. The consequence, that Unalaska is no longer a designated customs port of entry in Customs Collection District No. 31, is a surviving effect of an executed act and not an unperformed command.
